title: KCAS Bio and Scispot: Why Start With Scientific Reporting
summary: KCAS Bio is working with Scispot to automate scientific reporting first, with inventory, dose formulation analysis and connected workflows planned next.
body_markdown:
KCAS Bio is a global bioanalytical and biomarker CRO based in Olathe, Kansas. Its team of 380+ employees offers GLP- and GCP-compliant services from discovery through commercial approval, covering both large and small molecule work. KCAS Bio and Scispot have announced a partnership to advance KCAS Bio's digital transformation.


The partnership will initially focus on scientific reporting. A phased roadmap will then extend to inventory, dose formulation analysis and connected lab workflows. The decision to begin with reporting reflects the potential benefits of automation and connected records for KCAS Bio's scientists and sponsors.


## What the partnership covers


The partnership aims to help KCAS Bio's scientists spend less time on repetitive data handling and report preparation, allowing them to dedicate more time to analysis, interpretation and sponsor collaboration.


### Phase one: scientific reporting


Initial work focuses on automating scientific reporting. This is the first workflow KCAS Bio and Scispot plan to implement using Scispot's platform, establishing a foundation for the subsequent phases of the roadmap.


### What comes next


The roadmap then moves to inventory, dose formulation analysis and connected lab workflows. These initiatives remain planned work, and none of the subsequent phases has launched yet.


### How progress will be measured


KCAS Bio and Scispot will measure progress through workflow cycle time and capacity. These two measures maintain a focus on operational performance: how long a workflow takes and how much work the team can handle.


## Why reporting is the first workflow selected for automation


In a CRO, the report is a critical deliverable for sponsors. It brings together results, run details, sample information and review notes, often from multiple systems and spreadsheets. Manual data transfers introduce opportunities for transcription errors or outdated values, requiring additional verification.


Three factors make scientific reporting a practical starting point for automation.


### The work repeats


Reports in regulated laboratories follow standardized formats. Similar tables, checks and validation procedures are repeated across studies. These recurring processes are well suited to automation because established rules and requirements can guide their execution.


### The time goes back to the scientists


Report preparation takes skilled scientists away from scientific work. Automating the movement of data into reports can reduce manual copying and allow scientists to dedicate more time to analysis, interpretation and sponsor collaboration. Since improving scientific productivity is a central objective of the partnership, reporting presents a logical starting point.


### Reporting reveals gaps upstream


Automating scientific reporting requires a clear understanding of data provenance. Each reported value must be traceable to its originating sample, run, instrument and associated personnel. Establishing these connections for reporting also creates a foundation for the additional workflows included in the partnership roadmap.


## What connected records mean for traceability


Traceability is a straightforward concept that can be difficult to maintain manually. Reviewers and sponsors should be able to trace reported results back to their original sources. When records are distributed across disconnected files and systems, reconstructing that information can become a time-consuming process.


Connected records aim to maintain these relationships within a unified environment. Results remain linked to their supporting records, while documentation follows consistent structures and formats. KCAS Bio's digital transformation strategy places significant emphasis on these capabilities because connected records and standardized documentation support data integrity, traceability and scientific review.


### Built on KCAS Bio's quality systems


The partnership builds on KCAS Bio's existing quality systems and independent QA processes. Scispot's role is to connect data and automate the workflows surrounding these established systems. The objective is to ensure that records reach the review stage with supporting information already linked and consistently documented, providing QA teams with a clearer audit trail.


## Why this matters for sponsor trust


Sponsors select CRO partners based on scientific expertise and confidence in the reliability of the underlying data. John Bucksath, CEO of KCAS Bio, emphasized these priorities:


> "Our sponsors count on KCAS Bio for rigorous science, reliable data and a team that understands their development goals. Digital transformation is an investment in those commitments. Working with Scispot, we are building an operation that can support our clients' growing needs while keeping quality central to how we work."


Accessible and verifiable records can help sponsors understand how scientific results were generated. Guru Singh, founder and CEO of Scispot, described the partnership's objectives:


> "Digital transformation should make scientific work easier to execute and easier to verify. We are helping KCAS Bio connect its data and automate high-value workflows so its scientists can focus on the expertise sponsors depend on."


For sponsors, the partnership aims to preserve the rigorous scientific standards already associated with KCAS Bio while making supporting records more accessible and easier to verify during scientific review.

The full press release outlining the KCAS Bio and Scispot partnership is available[here](https://www.scispot.com/press-releases/kcas-bio-scispot-partnership) .


Laboratories evaluating reporting automation or connected records can[request a consultation](https://www.scispot.com/demo-request) with the Scispot team to explore potential opportunities for digital transformation.
